scenes.title: Before the lesson — four foundations
scenes.objective: Retrieve joint laws, marginals and conditional expectation.
body: A conditional distribution is the law of one random variable after another has been observed. The denominator is the marginal law of the observed variable; the support is the original joint support sliced at that value. Most errors are support errors, not integration errors.
A conditional distribution is a complete probability law. Its support and normalisation are part of the answer.

ask.q: Which marginal belongs in the denominator of f(X|Y=y)?
ask.nudge: Use the marginal of the variable whose value is observed.

items.recall: Integrate the joint density over x on the joint support.
refresh: To obtain the marginal density of Y, start from the joint density f(x,y) and integrate out X. For each fixed y, integrate across every x-value allowed by the joint support: f_Y(y)=∫ f(x,y) dx. The limits come from the support, not automatically from 0 to 1 or from the full real line.

After finding f_Y(y), check that it is a valid density: it must be non-negative and its integral over the full support of Y must equal 1. The support of Y is obtained by projecting the joint support onto the y-axis. A missing or incorrect limit changes the marginal and every conditional law built from it.

Conditional probability measures the chance of A after B is known to have occurred. Restrict the sample space to B, then count the part of B that also lies in A: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0. The denominator is the probability of the information you have been given.

For example, if 30 of 100 students take Statistics and 12 of those 30 also take Economics, then P(Economics|Statistics)=12/30, not 12/100. The latter is the joint probability. Conditioning changes the reference group, so always identify the event after the vertical bar before choosing the denominator.

A conditional expectation is an ordinary expectation under the conditional distribution. First obtain f_{X|Y}(x|y), including its support; then multiply the value g(x) by that conditional density and integrate: E[g(X)|Y=y]=∫g(x)f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx. For a discrete variable, replace the integral by a sum.

If g(x)=x, the result is the conditional mean. If g(x)=x², it gives the conditional second moment, from which Var(X|Y=y)=E(X²|Y=y)−{E(X|Y=y)}². The integration limits must be the conditional support at the observed y, not the unconditional support of X.

items.recall: The conditional law equals the marginal law almost everywhere.
refresh: Independence means that learning Y does not change the probability law of X. In distributional terms, for almost every y with positive marginal density, f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_X(x) on the relevant support; in the discrete case, use the corresponding conditional and marginal pmfs. The equality is about the whole distribution, not just equal means.

A useful test is to derive the conditional law and see whether y remains in it. If the conditional density or pmf changes with y, the variables are not independent. If it simplifies to the marginal law for almost every admissible y, that is the independence condition. Do not confuse zero covariance with independence unless an additional result, such as joint normality, applies.

scenes.title: The support is a moving slice
body: A joint density lives on a region in the plane. Conditioning fixes one coordinate and leaves a one-dimensional slice.
The joint density is divided by the marginal density of the fixed coordinate. This rescales the slice so its total probability is one.
When the support is triangular, the slice changes with the observed value. That is why support must be written explicitly.

scenario.teaser: A technician observes a batch score and updates an individual measurement.
scenario.title: Conditioning changes the range
body: The joint model has density 2 on 0<y<x<1. Observing X=x cuts the triangle to 0<Y<x.
The marginal is f_X(x)=2x, so the conditional density is 1/x on (0,x). It is uniform, with mean x/2.
Reversing the condition gives X|Y=y uniform on (y,1), with mean (1+y)/2. The direction matters: the two laws are not interchangeable.
The lesson is operational: identify the observed variable, slice the joint support, compute its marginal and only then divide.
scenario.q: Why are the two conditional supports different?
scenario.answer: Fixing X=x leaves 0<Y<x; fixing Y=y leaves y<X<1. Each condition slices the triangle in a different direction.

ask.q: What is the most common source of error in a conditional-density derivation?
ask.nudge: The ratio is short; the support limits are where the problem changes.

blocks.body: p_{X|Y}(x|y)=p(x,y)/p_Y(y); f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f(x,y)/f_Y(y). Divide by the marginal of the variable being conditioned on.
For 0<y<x<1, fixing X=x leaves 0<Y<x; fixing Y=y leaves y<X<1. The two conditional laws are directional.
For every admissible y, ∫f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx=1 over the conditional support. This is the fastest check for an algebra or support error.
X and Y are independent iff f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_X(x) almost everywhere (or the pmf analogue). A conditional law that changes with y signals dependence.
X|Y=y is normal with mean μ_X+ρ(σ_X/σ_Y)(y−μ_Y) and variance σ_X²(1−ρ²). The variance does not depend on y.

scenes.title: Conditional normal distributions
scenes.objective: Use the bivariate normal conditional formulas.

blocks.body: E(X|Y=y)=μ_X+ρ(σ_X/σ_Y)(y−μ_Y). The conditional mean shifts linearly with y.
Var(X|Y=y)=σ_X²(1−ρ²). It does not depend on y.
For a jointly normal pair, X|Y=y is normal with the mean and variance above. Zero correlation implies independence within the bivariate normal family.

ask.nudge: Compare the conditional mean and variance.

scenes.title: On your own — bivariate normal conditioning
scenes.problem: For a bivariate normal pair with μ_X=10, μ_Y=20, σ_X=4, σ_Y=5, ρ=0.6, find X|Y=15 and P(X≤10|Y=15).
scenes.check: The conditional mean is 7.6, not the marginal mean 10. The conditional variance remains 10.24.

scenario.teaser: A researcher inserts the observed value into the conditional variance formula.
scenario.title: Conditional normal distribution
body: For a bivariate normal pair, the conditional mean shifts linearly with the observed value.
With the stated parameters and Y=15, the mean is 7.6. The variance is 16(1−0.36)=10.24 and is constant in y.
This is a special property of the bivariate normal family; do not generalise constant conditional variance to arbitrary joint distributions.
scenario.q: What changes with y in the bivariate normal conditional law?
scenario.answer: The conditional mean changes linearly with y; the conditional variance is constant in y.

solution.why: The conditional mean changes with observed Y.
The conditional variance is constant in y.

scenes.title: Six claims — decide before revealing
scenes.objective: Catch support, denominator and independence errors.

items.claim: The denominator of f(X|Y=y) is f_X(x).
items.why: False: it is f_Y(y), the marginal of the conditioning variable.

items.claim: Conditional support is the joint support sliced at the observed value.
items.why: True: fixing Y=y leaves only compatible x-values.

items.claim: A conditional density integrates to one over its conditional support.

items.why: False: the conditioning variables and supports differ.

items.claim: For a bivariate normal pair, Var(X|Y=y) depends on y.
items.why: False: it is σ_X²(1−ρ²), independent of y.

items.claim: Independence is equivalent to conditional law equalling marginal law almost everywhere.

scenes.title: Transfer problem — reverse the conditioning
scenes.objective: Apply marginalisation and normalisation to a new slice.
scenes.problem: For f(x,y)=2 on 0<y<x<1, find f_{X|Y}(x|y) and E(X|Y=y).
hints: Integrate over x from y to 1 to obtain f_Y(y).
At fixed y, x ranges from y to 1.
Integrate x times the conditional density.
scenes.answer: f_Y(y)=2(1−y); f_{X|Y}=1/(1−y) on y<x<1; X|Y=y~Uniform(y,1), so E(X|Y=y)=(1+y)/2.
scenes.check: The density integrates to one over an interval of length 1−y. Do not use support 0<x<y.

solution.why: It integrates to one over length 1−y.
The mean of a uniform law is its interval midpoint.

items.q: What is the denominator of f(X|Y)?

items.a: The x-values compatible with the joint support when Y=y.

items.q: When are X and Y independent?
items.a: When the conditional law equals the marginal law almost everywhere.
